offence_severity: Minimum 6 months to maximum 2 years imprisonment and fine under s. 498A and s. 506 IPC
physical_harm: Mental and physical trauma caused to the wife
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the FIR was vague, general and sweeping, specifying no instances of criminal conduct, and that it was filed nearly 2 years after the divorce petition and 6 months after the domestic violence case by the mother-in-law, indicating it was filed to harass the appellant and his family members.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses' credibility by noting that the allegations levelled in the FIR were general and sweeping without specific instances of criminal conduct, and that the FIR was a counterblast to the divorce petition and domestic violence case.

legal_representation.state: Chritarth Palli, Dr. Monika Gusain, Parveen Kumar Aggarwal, Abhishek Grover, Vivek Gupta, Vikas Gupta, Advs.

appeal_history.high_court: High Court declined to quash the criminal proceedings
appeal_history.supreme_court: Appeal allowed, High Court's impugned judgment and order set aside

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the FIR and chargesheet indicated the appellant and his family members had allegedly demanded dowry and caused mental and physical trauma to the first informant-wife, thereby constituting cognizable offences under sections 323, 406, 498A and 506 of the IPC.
defence_argument: The appellant argued that the FIR was vague, general and sweeping, with no specific instances of criminal conduct, and that the allegations were a counterblast to the divorce petition and domestic violence case, with no genuine intent to commit an offence.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that the inherent power under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. should be exercised sparingly, carefully and with caution, only where such exercise is justified by the tests laid down in the Section itself, and that the court has the power to prevent abuse of the process of the court or miscarriage of justice.
precedent_relied_upon: R.P. Kapur v. State of Punjab, AIR 1960 SC 866; State of A.P. v. Vangaveeti Nagaiah [2009] 6 SCR 160 : (2009) 12 SCC 466 : AIR 2009 SC 2646; Preeti Gupta v. State of Jharkhand [2010] 9 SCR 1168 : 2010 Criminal Law Journal 4303 (1); Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar [2014] 8 SCR 128 : Crl.A.No.1277 of 2014 decided on 02.07.2014; Geeta Mehrotra & Anr. v. State of U.P. [2012] 9 SCR 641 : (2012) 10 SCC 741; State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal [1990] Supp 3 SCR 259 : [1992] Supp. (1) SCC 335; Mahmood Ali & Ors. v. State of U.P & Ors., 2023 SCC OnLine SC 950
other_sentence_order: The Supreme Court quashed the criminal proceedings, directed the Registry to send a copy of the judgment to the Union Law Secretary and Union Home Secretary, and requested the Legislature to consider making necessary changes in Sections 85 and 86 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
